title: Al-Mutaffifin: the rust on hearts
hook: what they earned has rusted over their hearts (83:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Mutaffifin, and the two rulers, full for me, short for you. Your line was full measure.

Leave a bike out in the rain for one night and nothing happens. Leave it out all winter and you come back to a chain that won't turn. Rust doesn't arrive in a day. It comes a speck at a time, each speck too small to bother with, until the thing doesn't move anymore. Al-Mutaffifin uses that same picture, one anyone who's owned something metal will know, for what a tiny cheat, repeated, does: not to the customer, but to the one doing it.
screen: `ONE NIGHT IN THE RAIN.` → `A WHOLE WINTER.` → `THE RUST ON HEARTS.`

segments.voice: The surah describes people who hear its verses recited and say: stories of the ancients. Old tales, nothing to do with me. Verse fourteen explains why, in Pickthall's words: Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts. The Arabic word is rana, a covering, a film, a crust that forms over something and dulls it. It isn't that they can't hear. What they've done has built up, layer on layer, until the heart doesn't catch the light anymore. A hadith in Tirmidhi turns the verse into a picture. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that when a person does wrong, a black spot is put on the heart. If he stops, asks forgiveness and turns back, the heart is polished clean. If he goes back to it, the spot grows, until it covers the heart. And that, he said, is the rana that God mentions. So the picture has two halves: hearts rust, and hearts shine. Turning back, tawbah, is the polish. So is remembrance of God, which some scholars describe as the heart's cleaning cloth. The man skimming a pinch off every sale doesn't feel like a villain. Each pinch is a speck. But the specks add up, not only in the ledger but in him, until the verses sound like old stories. And a few verses later the surah describes the other record, of the righteous, and says: for this, let those who compete, compete.
screen: `STORIES OF THE ANCIENTS.` · `RANA — A CRUST THAT DULLS.` · `A BLACK SPOT, OR POLISHED CLEAN.` · `LET THOSE WHO COMPETE, COMPETE.` · then, large: `HEARTS RUST; HEARTS SHINE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small habit that's been building up quietly, a little dishonesty, a daily irritation you feed, a thing you keep meaning to stop, and picture it as one spot on something that should shine. Then picture a cloth, and one slow wipe. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, I seek God's forgiveness.
Al-Mutaffifin. Those who skim, Surah eighty-three, which says what they earned became rust on their hearts. Today's word.
Your line: hearts rust; hearts shine. In the hadith, the rust can still come off. Day two hundred nine.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of polishing the heart through tawbah, turning back, and dhikr, remembrance; saying astaghfirullah, I seek God's forgiveness, through the day is one way this is done, recalling the hadith of the black spot that is wiped clean.

original.note: Arabic: "covered over, rusted," a crust that dulls a surface (Qur'an 83:14).

trapdoor: what you thought: bad deeds make a bad heart.
what it means: small wrongs repeated form a crust over the heart until even the verses sound like old stories; turning back polishes it.

what a scholar hears: some scholars distinguish rana, ghayn and tab' as degrees of covering; Tirmidhi 3334 is the hadith of the black spot; asatir al-awwalin, tales of the ancients, is a dismissal the Qur'an quotes in several surahs.
